title: Halving the search
objectives: Implement binary search and handle its edge cases.
Find the leftmost index at or above a target, and use `bisect_left` and `bisect_right`.

screens.title: One look
screens.prose: Sixteen closing prices, in pounds, sorted from low to high. You want to know whether £64 is among them. You may look at one cell first.
screens.question: Tap the cell whose value rules out the most cells, whatever it turns out to be.

hints.text: If the cell you look at is below 64, which cells can you forget?
Looking here leaves only one side in play, and each side is about half.
Look in the middle, at index 7 or 8. Either way, about half the cells are ruled out.

feedback.correct: The middle cell splits the list into two halves of about eight.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the cell that leaves the fewest cells in play.

byKey.c0: You looked at the first cell. If it is not 64, it rules out only itself.
byKey.c15: You looked at the last cell. If it is not 64, it rules out only itself.
byKey.c12: You looked at 64's own cell, from knowing the answer. With values unseen, a miss there leaves 12 cells in play.

explain.text: Index 7 holds £35. Because the list is sorted, 64 cannot be at index 7 or anywhere left of it. One look rules out eight cells.

ops.label: 64 is left of mid: `hi = mid - 1`
ops.why: You kept the left part, but 58 is below 64. Everything left of 58 is smaller still.

w1.tex: \text{every value left of index 11 is below } 58

This is the cell you are looking at now.
35 and 58 are below 64, so go right twice. 70 is above 64, so go left. Then mid lands on 64.

byKey.w0: You kept the left half, but 35 is below 64. In a sorted list, 64 sits right of 35.
byKey.w1: You kept the left part, but 58 is below 64. Go right of it.

explain.text: Each look halved the cells in play: 16, then 8, then 4, then 1. Four looks found 64 among 16 prices. A scan from the left would have needed 13.

screens.title: A million prices
screens.prose: This is **binary search**. Each look halves what is left, so the looks grow like $\log_2 n$: we write $O(\log n)$. The table counts the most looks it can take.

state.caption: Worst case: the value is absent or found last

screens.question: How many looks can binary search need on 1,000,000 sorted prices?

hints.text: How many times can you halve 1,000,000 before one item is left?
Sixteen items need 5 looks, and $2^4 = 16$.
$2^{19} = 524{,}288$ and $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$. So 19 halvings get below 2 items, and one more look checks it: 20.

feedback.correct: Twenty looks, against a million for a scan.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count halvings, not items.

byKey.scan: You counted a scan of every price. Binary search throws away half at each look.
byKey.half: You counted half the list, the average for a scan. Binary search halves again and again.
byKey.log: You took $\log_2 10^6 \approx 19.9$ and rounded down. The last item left still needs one look of its own.

explain.text: The worst case needs $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ looks. For a million that is $19 + 1 = 20$. Doubling the list adds just one look.

screens.title: Write the search
screens.prose: Turn the steps into code. Return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it is not there. Test 11 counts your looks in a list of a million: at most 25.

state.caption: `lo` and `hi` start at the two ends

screens.question: Write `binary_search(xs, target)` for a sorted list `xs`.

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests: the ends, an empty list, one element, targets below, above and between the values, duplicates, and two searches of a million values that count your looks.

hints.text: Start with `lo, hi = 0, len(xs) - 1` and loop while there is a cell left between them.
On the first pass `mid` is index 7.
`while lo <= hi:` set `mid = (lo + hi) // 2`. Return `mid` on a match; else move `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`. After the loop, return `-1`.

feedback.correct: Every case passes, in at most 21 looks for a million values.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 searches an empty list. With `hi = len(xs) - 1 = -1` the loop should not run at all.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 is a single element. If you wrote `while lo < hi`, the loop never looks at it.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 counts looks. More than 25 means you scanned the list instead of halving it.

explain.text: `while lo <= hi` runs while at least one cell is in play, so a single element is checked. `lo = mid + 1` and `hi = mid - 1` always shrink the range. When they cross, the target is absent.

screens.title: The first one
screens.prose: Now find the **first** index where `xs[i] >= 4`. Here `hi` starts at `len(xs)`, one past the end. The answer is always in the range from `lo` to `hi`.

`lo = mid + 1`: look right of mid
ops.why: You went right, but `xs[4]` is not below 4. The first 4 is at index 4 or to its left.

ops.label: `lo = mid + 1`
ops.why: You went right, but `xs[2]` is not below 4. The first 4 is at index 2 or to its left.

ops.label: `lo = mid + 1`
ops.why: You went right, but `xs[1]` is not below 4. The first 4 is at index 1 or to its left.

ops.why: You kept index 0, but `xs[0] = 2` is below 4. It cannot be the first 4.

hints.text: When `xs[mid]` is a 4, could it be the first 4?
A 4 at mid might be the first one, so mid must stay in play.
On a 4, set `hi = mid`, keeping mid. On a value below 4, set `lo = mid + 1`. Stop when `lo == hi`.

feedback.correct: `lo` and `hi` met at index 1, the first 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep mid in play whenever it holds a 4.

byKey.stop: You stopped at the first 4 you met. There are 4s further left, and you want the first.
byKey.wr: You went right of a 4. The first 4 is never right of another 4.
byKey.wl: You kept index 0, but it holds 2, which is below 4.

explain.text: A 4 at mid might be the first, so `hi = mid` keeps it. A value below 4 cannot be, so `lo = mid + 1` drops it. When `lo` meets `hi`, that index is the answer.

screens.title: Leftmost at least
screens.prose: Return the leftmost index `i` with `xs[i] >= target`. If every value is smaller, return `len(xs)`, the place where `target` would be inserted.

state.caption: `hi = len(xs) = 8` sits one past the end

screens.question: Write `first_at_least(xs, target)` for a sorted list `xs`.

tests.setup: import bisect, random; rng = random.Random(7); data = sorted(rng.randrange(50) for _ in range(200))
tests.call: all(first_at_least(data, t) == bisect.bisect_left(data, t) for t in range(-2, 53))

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests: duplicates, a target between two values, below and above every value, an empty list, all values equal, a million values with your looks counted, and 55 targets checked against `bisect.bisect_left`.

hints.text: Copy the stepping you just did: `lo, hi = 0, len(xs)` and loop `while lo < hi`.
When every value is below `target`, the answer is this end position, `len(xs)`.
If `xs[mid] < target`, set `lo = mid + 1`; else set `hi = mid`. Return `lo` after the loop.

feedback.correct: Every case passes, and it agrees with `bisect_left` on all 55 targets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has three 2s and expects index 1. Returning on the first 2 you meet gives the middle one.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 expects 3, one past the end. Start with `hi = len(xs)`, not `len(xs) - 1`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has all values equal and a larger target. The answer is `len(xs)`, 4.

explain.text: This is exactly `bisect.bisect_left(xs, target)` from the standard library. `bisect_right` is the same with `<=` in place of `<`: it returns the index after the last equal value. Both take $O(\log n)$ looks.

screens.title: It never returns
screens.question: Why does the loop never end?

options.text: With `hi = lo + 1`, `mid` equals `lo`, and `lo = mid` leaves `lo` where it was
`while lo < hi` should be `while lo <= hi`
options.why: You changed the loop condition. With `<=` the loop would also keep running once `lo == hi`, so it gets worse, not better.
You blamed overflow. Python integers never overflow; that bug lives in C and Java, where `lo + hi` can pass the largest `int`.

options.text: 35 is not in the list, so the search goes on for ever
options.why: You blamed the missing value. A correct search returns 3 here, the place 35 would go.

hints.text: Work out `mid` when `lo = 2` and `hi = 3`.
Both `lo` and `mid` point at this cell.
`mid = (2 + 3) // 2 = 2`. 30 is below 35, so `lo = mid = 2`. Nothing changed, so the next pass is the same.

feedback.correct: `lo = mid` makes no progress once two cells are left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace one more pass from `lo = 2`, `hi = 3`.

byKey.cond: You changed the condition. The problem is the update: `lo = mid` can leave `lo` where it was.
byKey.overflow: You blamed overflow. Python integers grow as needed. The loop is stuck because `lo` stops moving.
byKey.absent: You blamed the missing value. An absent target is fine; the loop is stuck because `lo` never moves.

explain.text: Floor division rounds `mid` down, so with two cells left `mid == lo`. Then `lo = mid` changes nothing and the loop spins. Write `lo = mid + 1`: `xs[mid]` is too small, so it can never be the answer.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
The invariant: everything left of `lo` is below `target`, and everything from `hi` on is at least `target`.

```python
lo, hi = 0, len(xs)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if xs[mid] < target:
        lo = mid + 1
    else:
        hi = mid
return lo
```

Each pass halves the range, so at most $\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$ passes.
screens.question: This loop uses `lo = mid + 1` and `hi = mid`. Which condition must it use?

options.why: With `<=`, the loop runs once more when `lo == hi`. Then `mid == hi` and `hi = mid` changes nothing, so it never ends.
This stops with two cells still in play. You would need an extra check after the loop.

feedback.correct: `hi = mid` goes with `while lo < hi`; `hi = mid - 1` goes with `while lo <= hi`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens on the pass where `lo == hi`.

explain.text: Both pairings work: `lo <= hi` with `hi = mid - 1`, or `lo < hi` with `hi = mid`. Mixing them loops for ever or skips a cell. In C or Java write `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, because `lo + hi` can overflow there.

screens.title: Days below a level
screens.prose:
To count the days a stock closed below a level, sort a copy of the closes once. Then each question is one bisection.

```python
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
s = sorted(closes)
bisect_left(s, 100)   # 3
```
screens.question: What does `bisect_right(s, 100)` return?

hints.text: `bisect_right` returns the index just after the last value equal to 100.
These are the three closes of exactly £100.
The 100s sit at indices 3, 4 and 5. The index after the last one is 6.

feedback.correct: Six days closed at or below £100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the index just after the last 100.

byKey.left: You gave `bisect_left`, the index of the first 100. `bisect_right` goes past the equal values.
byKey.last: You gave the index of the last 100. `bisect_right` returns the index after it.
byKey.count: You counted the days above £100. `bisect_right` counts from the left.

explain.text: `bisect_left(s, 100) = 3` counts closes strictly below £100. `bisect_right(s, 100) = 6` counts closes at or below it. After one $O(n \log n)$ sort, each level costs $O(\log n)$.

screens.title: The next trading day
screens.prose: A backtest wants the first trading day on or after a given date. Trading days are ISO date strings, sorted, and ISO strings sort in date order.

state.caption: Trading days in March 2026 (month-day); 7 and 8 March are a weekend

screens.question: Write `next_trading_day(days, day)`: the first entry of `days` on or after `day`, or `None` if there is none.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests: a weekend, a trading day itself, a date before the first day, a date after the last, the last day, and an empty calendar.

hints.text: Which function returns the first index with `days[i] >= day`?
Saturday 7 March is not a trading day; this is the next one.
`i = bisect_left(days, day)`. If `i == len(days)`, return `None`; else return `days[i]`.

feedback.correct: One bisection per lookup, and the end of the calendar returns `None`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 asks for a trading day itself. `bisect_right` skips past an equal date; use `bisect_left`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 asks for a date after the last trading day. `bisect_left` returns `len(days)` there, so return `None`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 passes an empty list. `bisect_left` returns 0, which equals `len(days)`, so return `None`.

explain.text: `bisect_left` finds the first day not before `day`, which is the definition we want. Past the last day it returns `len(days)`, which must not be used as an index. Over ten years of days that is 12 looks per lookup.

ideas: On a sorted list, one look at the middle rules out half of what is left.
Keep an invariant: the answer always lies between `lo` and `hi`, and every pass must shrink that range.
`bisect_left` gives the first index at or above a value, `bisect_right` the index after the last equal one.

formula.name: Looks in the worst case
formula.note: A million sorted values need at most 20 looks.

summary.trap: `lo = mid` without `+ 1` stops the range shrinking once two cells are left, and the loop never ends.

quiz.prose:
```python
binary_search([8, 3, 12, 5, 20], 5)
```
This is the `binary_search` you wrote, given a list that is not sorted.
quiz.question: What does it return?

options.why: You found 5 by reading the whole list. The search looks only at 12, then 8, and both send it left.
Nothing in the code checks that the list is sorted. It halves anyway and returns an answer.
Index 0 holds 8. The search looks there but 8 is not 5.

feedback.correct: It misses 5, because the list is not sorted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace `lo`, `mid` and `hi` by hand.

explain.text: First `mid = 2` holds 12, above 5, so `hi = 1`. Then `mid = 0` holds 8, above 5, so `hi = -1` and the loop ends. Binary search is only correct on sorted data.

quiz.prose: A sorted list holds 5,000 option strikes.
quiz.question: At most how many looks does binary search need?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the power of two just below 5,000.

byKey.floor: You took $\lfloor \log_2 5000 \rfloor = 12$. The last item left needs one more look.
byKey.half: You counted half the list, as a scan would. Each look halves what is left.

explain.text: $2^{12} = 4096 \le 5000 < 8192 = 2^{13}$, so $\lfloor \log_2 5000 \rfloor = 12$. The worst case is $12 + 1 = 13$ looks.

quiz.prose:
```python
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
s = [1, 3, 3, 3, 8]
print(bisect_left(s, 3), bisect_right(s, 3))
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You gave the index of the last 3 for `bisect_right`. It returns the index after it.
You gave 0 for `bisect_left`, but `s[0] = 1` is below 3. The first 3 is at index 1.
You gave the middle 3 twice. The two functions return the two ends of the run of 3s.

feedback.correct: The run of 3s starts at 1 and ends just before 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the run of 3s starts and ends.

explain.text: `bisect_left` gives the first index holding 3, which is 1. `bisect_right` gives the index after the last 3, which is 4. Their difference, 3, counts the 3s.

quiz.prose:
`first_at_least` returns the leftmost index `i` with `xs[i] >= target`, or `len(xs)`.

```python
first_at_least([5, 5, 5, 5], 5)
```
quiz.question: What does it return?

options.why: You gave the last 5. The leftmost index with a value of at least 5 is the first one.
You gave the first `mid` looked at. The search keeps going left while it sees 5s.
You gave `len(xs)`, the answer when every value is too small. Here `xs[0]` already qualifies.

feedback.correct: Every value is at least 5, so the first index wins.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which is the leftmost index holding at least 5?

explain.text: Every pass sees a 5, so `hi = mid` moves left each time: `hi` goes 2, 1, 0. The loop stops at `lo = hi = 0`.
